content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the typical properties of metals and non-metals
Explain the properties of metals in terms of structure and bonding
Identify metals and non-metals from their properties
Explain what metalloids are and give examples
The elements in the Periodic Table can be broadly classified as
based on their physical and chemical properties. About 80% of elements are metals. Understanding the differences between metals and non-metals helps us predict how they will behave.
Most metals share these typical properties:
Most are solid at room temperature (except mercury)
Make a ringing sound when struck
Form positive ions (cations) by losing electrons
React with oxygen to form basic oxides
React with acids to form salts and hydrogen
Insulators of heat and electricity (except graphite)
Often gases or low-melting solids at room temperature
Form negative ions (anions) by gaining electrons, or share electrons
React with oxygen to form acidic oxides
Do not react with dilute acids
The properties of metals are explained by
Metal atoms lose their outer electrons
These electrons become delocalised (free to move throughout the structure)
Positive metal ions are held in a "sea" of delocalised electrons
Delocalised electrons can move and carry charge
Layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking
are elements with properties of both metals and non-metals. They are found along the stepped line in the Periodic Table.
Conduct electricity better at higher temperatures
Silicon and germanium are used in electronic components (computer chips, solar cells) because they are semiconductors.
Left side and centre (most of the table)
Along the stepped line dividing metals and non-metals
Special case - a non-metal placed with Group 1
Cooking pans (aluminium, copper) - good thermal conductors
Fuels (carbon compounds) - release energy when burned
Solar cells (silicon, germanium) - convert light to electricity
Thinking all metals are hard and strong
Some metals are soft (sodium can be cut with a knife) and some have low melting points (mercury is liquid at room temperature)
Non-metals can be solids (carbon, sulfur), liquids (bromine), or gases (oxygen, nitrogen)
Saying carbon conducts electricity, so it's a metal
Only graphite (a form of carbon) conducts; diamond doesn't. Carbon is a non-metal with unusual properties.
Metals are typically shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and are malleable and ductile
Non-metals are typically dull, poor conductors, and brittle if solid
Metal properties are explained by delocalised electrons in metallic bonding
Metalloids have properties of both metals and non-metals
Metals form positive ions; non-metals form negative ions
Metals are on the left of the Periodic Table; non-metals on the right
